name: Carlos Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at the contact centre look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get the queue at eight, mostly billing calls and chats, then take the cases the newer agents cannot settle. I am a team lead, but my own pay is still at the lower end here. I like talking somebody down from a bad morning; I hate watching the clock while I do it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the part you take home with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The quality reports. I have a two-year college diploma and I know these accounts well, yet one long call can make the numbers look poor. I rent a small flat by myself and have less than a month of expenses saved, so a bad shift feels bigger than it ought to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my team that the queue will still need us. A shorter call summary might give us a few minutes back, but customers still want a person who can sort a wrong charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I would be relieved, though I would not say that in front of the new hires. My rent already eats too much of my lower pay. A quiet AI year does not put money into my savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking the hard billing calls and check any machine summary before I close a case. Starting now, I would put a fixed amount from each pay into a separate rent reserve, even if it is small. In the first year of this picture, I would keep the same schedule and skip replacing my old phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly steady about my job, but not about my bank balance. The phone could break before I save a month of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the agents you lead when they ask whether the software replaces them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a summary tool is not the same as handling a customer who has been charged twice. I would also tell them to read every summary, because I will be the one correcting the account later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which expense goes first if rent rises again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My rent gets a vote before my old phone does. The new phone goes first, even though its battery hardly lasts a shift. My sister keeps telling me to replace it, but rent gets the vote.

say: I would tell the team **people** still settle the hard billing calls.
I would say the new **summaries** need checking.
think: I am **relieved** my lead role stays useful.
I still have less than a month of **savings** to cover rent or a broken phone.
do: Keep taking **billing** escalations and check each machine summary.
Put a fixed amount from each pay into a **rent reserve**.
Delay replacing my **phone** during the first year.
feel: **Uneasy** about rent and a thin reserve.
S0.quote: My rent gets a vote before my old phone does.
fieldNote: His public confidence rests on the **hard calls** he handles.
The old **phone** is his first planned sacrifice when rent presses.
He does not confuse steady work with a comfortable **household budget**.

steps.text: Keep handling difficult billing calls and check machine case summaries
Transfer a fixed amount from each pay into a rent reserve
Delay replacing his old phone for the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the floor to learn the new answer system before it starts making our rosters. We should be the people who can spot a bad answer and explain a charge, not simply repeat the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think fewer easy calls means fewer seats. I am among the best on my team, yet the company could make one lead watch twice as many chats. There are few other contact centres nearby. My rent does not wait while I become good at a new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would ask my manager for access to the trial answer tool and keep a list of its mistakes on billing cases. I would spend two evenings a week learning the reporting side of our system. If hours fall in the first year, I would apply for the account review role here before I search farther away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious, especially when I picture an empty row of desks. Having something to learn keeps me from freezing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You tell the team to learn it, but you expect fewer seats. Which part do you say out loud?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say both, just not during a rushed handover. I would tell Ravi, the newest agent, that learning the tool gives him a better case for staying, not a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the internal move possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need a real vacancy and the same basic pay, or I cannot carry rent. I would ask the account review lead what skills they require before paying for any course.

say: I would tell the floor to **learn** the answer system.
I would ask agents to catch **wrong answers**.
think: I expect fewer **seats** even if the work stays busy.
I fear lost **hours** because rent takes much of my pay and few nearby jobs are available.
do: Test the **answer tool** on billing cases this month.
Apply for an **account-review vacancy** only if hours fall and basic pay matches my current rate.
S1.quote: My rent does not wait while I become good at a new screen.
fieldNote: He gives the team a practical **public line** while fearing cuts.
An internal move depends on a **vacancy** and enough pay to keep his flat.
He would ask the review lead for requirements before buying a **course**.

steps.text: Test the answer tool and log its billing mistakes this month
Study contact centre reporting two evenings a week
Apply for account review if hours fall and a vacancy matches current basic pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that we need a proper plan before management moves whole queues to AGI. Customers should know when a machine is making the decision, especially on a disputed bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the chats and most calls could go by 2028, and being a good lead might only mean I am kept for the last few complaints. The robots in 2031 do not change much for a desk like mine. My college diploma cannot pay the rent while a machine answers my calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the manager what work will stay with people and request training during paid hours, not on my own bill. I would set aside what I can each payday and ask my sister whether her spare room could be a short bridge if my job goes. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, I would take a paid account review opening if one exists; otherwise I would search beyond this town before agreeing to leave my flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds frightening because the date is close. I can name steps, but I cannot pretend they guarantee a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have pride in doing the hard calls. Would you tell your sister you might need her room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would hate that conversation, but I would have it before the rent is overdue. My sister would help for a while; she cannot pay my bills indefinitely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if my employer funds it or I can see a paid vacancy it qualifies me for. I have less than a month saved, so buying a vague certificate would be gambling with rent.

say: I would ask management for a **proper plan** before queues move.
I would tell customers when **AGI** decides their disputed bills.
think: I fear most of my calls could disappear by **2028**.
My **diploma** and thin savings cannot shield my wage through a rapid change.
do: Request **paid training** and a clear staffing plan now.
Ask my **sister** about a temporary spare room.
Seek a **paid vacancy** beyond town after 2028 if needed.
feel: I distrust any plan without a **wage**.
S2.quote: My college diploma cannot pay the rent while a machine answers my calls.
fieldNote: He distinguishes the 2028 **desk threat** from later robots.
His sister is a **bridge**, not a permanent subsidy for his rent.
He rejects a vague **certificate** without funding or a paid destination.

steps.text: Put affordable amounts from each pay into a rent reserve
Ask his sister about temporary use of her spare room
Search paid account review vacancies beyond town after 2028 if his job goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team that five years gives us room to ask for a fair path into the jobs that remain. I would want the company to show the roles and wages, not just promise that everyone will adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could use those years, but I still expect the answering side to shrink when AGI reaches it in 2031. I might be leading a smaller group or looking elsewhere before then. Robots around 2034 are a second clock for other workers; my calls face the first one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year, I would ask to shadow our account review lead one afternoon a month and learn the rules behind adjustments. I would build the reserve until it covers three months of rent and keep the phone another year. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I would apply to a real review or complaints role if the pay covers my flat; if none exists, I would look in the next city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried, though I can see a route through it. Five years is long enough to learn the rules properly if I do not waste the first one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your manager will not let you shadow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would ask for the written job requirements and learn what I can from cases I already handle. I would not quit to study full time with this little saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the phone for another year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months of rent would let me refuse a terrible offer. A new phone would look nice on the train and leave me with no choice at the station.

say: I would ask for **real roles** and wages.
I would use five years to prepare **properly** and ask what roles will remain.
think: My answering work still shrinks by **2031**.
A smaller team may mean a smaller **income** even if I keep my title.
do: Shadow the **account review** lead monthly, if allowed.
Apply for a **paid review role** after 2031 only if its wage covers my flat.
S3.quote: Three months of rent would let me refuse a terrible offer.
fieldNote: His condition for retraining is a **paid destination**.
He treats the phone as money for **choice** when a poor offer comes.
He would learn on current cases if shadowing is **refused**.

steps.text: Learn adjustment rules from monthly shadowing if allowed, or from current cases
Save toward three months of rent before AGI arrives
Keep his old phone for another year
Apply for review or complaints vacancies after 2031 only if pay covers my flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell younger agents that a decade is time to build a trade, not an excuse to ignore the screens. I would still ask the company what happens to the people who train the system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 37 when AGI arrives in 2036. I do not want to reach 37 with the same thin savings. My best calls may still be worth something before that date, but the desk work will change first. Robots around 2039 are not the reason I need a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would stay in the lead job and ask whether the firm will cover a part-time qualification in account rules or staff training. I would save steadily and take the internal training duties when they pay at least my current rate. In the first year after 2036, I would choose a paid training or complaints position if there is a vacancy; I would not resign just to chase a title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one leaves me uneasy rather than cornered. Ten years feels like enough time to become useful in a different corner of the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you from taking that qualification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm will not pay and there is no clear job at the end, I would stick to learning on the job. Rent still comes every month, even under the slow picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your sister to plan differently too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my sister to keep a reserve, but I would not tell her to choose a career because of my guesses. She knows her own work better than I do.

say: I would tell agents to build a **trade** over the decade.
I would ask who gains when staff **train systems**.
think: I refuse to reach **37** with the same thin savings.
My desk work changes before **robots** arrive, so I must prepare for 2036.
do: Save a larger **reserve** over the decade.
Take **internal training duties** only at my current rate; apply for posted training vacancies after 2036.
feel: A decade offers room to become **useful** elsewhere.
S4.quote: I do not want to reach 37 with the same thin savings.
fieldNote: He ties study to **funding** and a possible job.
He will not trade a current **wage** for a title without a real vacancy.
He connects the ten-year runway to becoming useful in **training** or complaints.

steps.text: Keep leading the contact centre team while preparing
Build a larger rent reserve over the decade
Take internal training duties only at current pay; seek posted training vacancies after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. A clear staffing plan, training on paid time and actual vacancies with wages I can live on would help. I do not need a speech about being flexible; I need to know whether my rent gets paid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who corrects a machine when it tells a customer the wrong balance. If the company still needs someone responsible, that job should have a name and a wage before the old jobs go.

headlineQuote: If the company still needs someone responsible, that job should have a name and a wage before the old jobs go.
portrait: Carlos is a **27-year-old** contact centre lead with a two-year college diploma.
He is among the **best agents**, yet earns lower pay and has less than a month saved.
Few nearby jobs make lost **hours** a direct rent threat.
He will learn proven tools, but wants **paid training** and a real vacancy before spending money.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove most calls before he can build a rent reserve.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **staffing plan**, paid training and vacancies with a livable wage would help.
